clue.text: Sauce bottles right at the double

indicators.note: to bottle something is to seal it inside a vessel, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: pesto is a basil and pine-nut sauce
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone rushes to empty sauce into bottles at top speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' reads as a plural noun but works as a verb: PESTO holds R, giving PRESTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Presto is a musical tempo marking meaning very quickly, matching an idiom for haste.

clue.text: More sexy am I when in control?

indicators.note: being placed inside something means these letters sit within the surrounding word

parts.note: to steer is to control direction
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether being in charge makes them more attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: The question reads as vanity about power; really AM I is placed inside STEER to make STEAMIER.
explanation.definitionFit: Steamy is informal for erotic or passionate, so its comparative describes something hotter and racier.

clue.text: Where the king's profile is correct

definitions.meaning: first meaning, literal: the monarch's head appears on coins and notes

explanation.surface: A question about where a monarch's portrait properly belongs.
explanation.walkthrough: British coins and banknotes carry the reigning monarch's head in profile, so the phrase is both a place and an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a guess or estimate that is precisely accurate, hitting the target exactly.

clue.text: Spying OAP, seeing wrinkly!

indicators.note: something wrinkled is creased and rumpled out of its original smooth shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pensioner caught snooping, with 'wrinkly' as a cheeky dig at their age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrinkly' is British slang for an old person, a neat fit with OAP (old-age pensioner), but here it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Espionage is the practice of gathering secret intelligence, the noun for covert surveillance work.

clue.text: Initially slowing first, come to a halt

indicators.note: at the start means only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: opening letter of the word
to be top is to be first

explanation.surface: Driving instructions: slow down first, then pull up completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' looks like an adverb of sequence, but it supplies TOP, as in top of the class.
explanation.definitionFit: To stop is a plain synonym for ceasing movement, bringing a vehicle or person to rest.

clue.text: Scout moved north in US city

indicators.note: something moved has been shifted from its place, so the letters change their order

parts.note: taken as written
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A boy scout relocates northwards to live in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moved north' reads as one relocation; really 'moved' rearranges the scout and N is added after.
explanation.definitionFit: Tucson is a large city in southern Arizona, an example of an American urban centre.

clue.text: Footwear worn by a decision maker — here without it?

definitions.note: 'it' points back to the footwear in the clue

indicators.note: clothing worn surrounds the wearer, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: a boot is a type of footwear
taken as written
a referee makes the decisions in a game

explanation.surface: A referee's boots, and the teasing question of whether he goes without them.
explanation.walkthrough: Grammatically the boot is worn by the official, but the letters go the other way, with the footwear wrapped round. The definition loops back to the footwear with 'it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being barefoot means having no shoes or socks on, so it describes someone lacking any footwear.

clue.text: Attendants confined to secure unit erroneously turned over

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the letters run backwards
something confined is kept within limits, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: Carers locked in a secure unit find their ward mistakenly upended.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts at the final E of 'secure' and ends at the R of 'erroneously'; read backwards it gives RETINUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is a body of followers or servants accompanying an important person, a collective for attendants.

clue.text: English or Irish poet removing cap takes lunch

indicators.note: taking off a cap removes the top, and in a down clue the top is the first letter

parts.note: Keats is an English poet; the Irish poet Yeats works equally well

explanation.surface: A poet doffs his hat and sits down to lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: Both KEATS and YEATS lose their first letter to leave the same word, which is why the setter can say 'English or Irish'.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat is to consume a meal, so the verb describes someone having their midday food.

clue.text: Put down the whole thing, a fruit

parts.note: past tense of sit in its sense of set or place down
a sum is a total, the whole amount
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sets the whole lot down and it turns out to be a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' suggests insulting or killing; here it is SAT, as in sat the child down.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a small, easy-peeling citrus fruit related to the mandarin, an example of a fruit.

clue.text: Food thrown at the pigs

indicators.note: something thrown is scattered and lands in disorder, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Leftover food is tossed to the pigs as swill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrown' reads as the verb in a farmyard scene; it is the signal to rearrange the three words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is a long thin pasta, a specific example of the general category of food.

clue.text: Out of the ark, go east

parts.note: to pass is to go by
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Animals leaving Noah's ark are told to head east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of the ark' is an idiom for very old-fashioned, as if dating from Noah's time, not an instruction to disembark.
explanation.definitionFit: Passé means outdated and no longer fashionable, matching the idiom for something antiquated.

clue.text: Hatred as leader removed from stage

indicators.note: taking away the leader means dropping the opening letter

parts.note: a podium is a raised stage or platform

explanation.surface: Public loathing as a political leader is ousted from the platform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' suggests a party leader being toppled; it is just the first letter of PODIUM.
explanation.definitionFit: Odium is general or widespread dislike and contempt, a formal synonym for strong loathing.

clue.text: Tory returned with love — absolutely not!

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Con is the short form of Conservative
and means together with
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A Conservative re-elected with affection, met by a flat refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' looks like a Tory MP re-elected; it reverses CON. A Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase is an emphatic refusal, saying something simply cannot be done.

clue.text: Mammal with icy beard, did you say?

indicators.note: asking what someone said points to how the words are pronounced rather than written

parts.note: a frozen beard chills the chin

explanation.surface: Someone asks about an animal with a frosty beard.
explanation.walkthrough: A beard covered in ice would be a 'chin chiller'; said in a non-rhotic accent, that matches the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The chinchilla is a small South American rodent prized for its soft fur, an example of a mammal.

clue.text: US state: name is not misspelt

indicators.note: a misspelt word has its letters wrongly placed, so they need reordering

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone insists the name of an American state has been spelt correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not misspelt' reads as a denial of error, but 'not' belongs to the fodder and 'misspelt' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Minnesota is a Midwestern American state bordering Canada, an example of one of the fifty.

clue.text: Mouse falling off girl

parts.note: to shrink is to fall off or diminish
Violet is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A rodent drops off a young girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouse' is a person here, a timid one, not the animal; 'falling off' means declining, not tumbling.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for an extremely shy, retiring person who avoids attention.

clue.text: Great cash

definitions.meaning: first meaning: excellent, of high quality

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as excited approval of money; the two words are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective praises sterling work as excellent, and the noun names the currency of the UK.

clue.text: Sweet in lounge I try

parts.note: to loll is to lounge lazily
taken as written
to have a pop at something is to have a try

explanation.surface: Someone samples a candy while sitting in the lounge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lounge' looks like a room and 'in' like a place word, but 'lounge' is a verb and 'in' merely links.
explanation.definitionFit: A lollipop is a hard candy on a stick, an example of a sweet, the British word for candy.

clue.text: Faculty attached to French city in one's formative years?

parts.note: hearing is one of the faculties, or senses
Lyon is a major city in France

explanation.surface: A university faculty linked to a French city, in its early days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faculty' suggests a university department; here it is one of the senses. The question mark flags a loose definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Formative years are those at the start of life, so the phrase meaning at an early stage fits.

clue.text: Negligent in relation to blunder

parts.note: re means concerning or in relation to
a miss is a failure or mistake

explanation.surface: Someone is careless when it comes to a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the familiar business-letter word for 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Remiss means careless in fulfilling a duty, a close synonym for failing to take proper care.

clue.text: Personality spotted in Venice, LeBlanc

indicators.note: something spotted inside a place is sitting within it, so the letters are found inside the words

parts.note: letters straddling the comma

explanation.surface: A famous person is sighted in Venice: someone called LeBlanc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' suggests paparazzi sighting a star, which fits the answer neatly; the letters run from the end of 'Venice' into 'LeBlanc'.
explanation.definitionFit: Celeb is informal for celebrity, and a personality can mean a famous public figure.

clue.text: Old car explosive?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for a battered old vehicle
second meaning: a firework that goes off with a loud noise

explanation.walkthrough: 'Explosive' reads as an adjective describing the car, perhaps a backfiring one, but it is a separate noun. In Britain a banger is a clapped-out car, and also a firecracker.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang word names a dilapidated vehicle and also a noisy firework that detonates with a bang.

clue.text: Pull tie

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to drag or haul
second meaning: a game ending level

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an instruction to tug a necktie; 'tie' is the sporting sense of a level result.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means haul something along, and the noun is a match in which neither side wins.

clue.text: Yellow lines everywhere, motorists often narked originally

indicators.note: the origin of each word is its start, so only opening letters are kept

parts.note: opening letters of the five words

explanation.surface: Parking restrictions are everywhere and drivers are fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain yellow lines painted along the kerb restrict parking, so 'Yellow' seems part of the scene; it is the definition. Narked is British slang for annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemon names a pale bright shade, the colour of the citrus fruit, a sense of yellow.

clue.text: Season in which Trotsky arose?

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from the bottom up, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Leon Trotsky, the Russian revolutionary

explanation.surface: A history question: at what time of year did Trotsky's uprising happen?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arose' suggests the Russian revolution's rising; in a down answer it turns LEON upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel is another word for Christmas, the festive period sometimes called the season.

clue.text: Islander in rain, sad unfortunately

indicators.note: things going unfortunately go wrong, so the letters end up in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An island dweller is miserable in the downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a place word, but its letters belong to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sardinian is a native of Sardinia, the large Mediterranean island, so is an example of an islander.

clue.text: Sea town crumbling easily

definitions.note: an adverb; the phrase is used adverbially, as in 'did it, no sweat'

indicators.note: something crumbling falls apart into fragments, so the letters are broken up and reformed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A coastal town erodes away without much resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Easily' seems to describe how the town crumbles, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase means without effort or difficulty, an idiom for doing something effortlessly.

clue.text: Old politician we found gathering everyone in around Post Office

indicators.note: to gather is to take things in, so the outer piece encloses what follows

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: going around something encircles it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: all means everyone
PO is the abbreviation for Post Office

explanation.surface: A veteran politician rounds everyone up at the post office.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two layers of wrapping, one inside the other. Robert Walpole is regarded as Britain's first Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Robert Walpole led the British government in the eighteenth century, an example of a statesman from long ago.
